text: Oprah Gail Winfrey (/ˈoʊprə/; born Orpah Gail Winfrey; January 29, 1954) is an American talk show host, television producer, actress, author, and media proprietor. She is best known for her talk show, The Oprah Winfrey Show, which aired in national syndication from Chicago from 1986 to 2011, spanning 25 years. Globally, she is the richest Black woman and the wealthiest female celebrity. Dubbed the "Queen of All Media," she was the richest African-American of the 20th century and once the world's only Black billionaire. By 2007, she was frequently ranked as the most influential woman in the world. Winfrey was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi, to a teenaged mother, Vernita Lee, and father Vernon Winfrey; her parents never married. Her mother worked as a housemaid, and her father was a coal miner who later became a barber and city councilman. A 2006 genetic test revealed her matrilineal ancestry originated among the Kpelle ethnic group from Liberia, with 89% Sub-Saharan African, 8% Native American, and 3% East Asian heritage. After birth, her mother moved north, and Winfrey lived in rural poverty with her maternal grandmother, Hattie Mae Lee, who taught her to read before age three and nicknamed her "The Preacher" for reciting Bible verses. Her grandmother beat her daily and often dressed her in potato sack dresses, which other children mocked. At age six, Winfrey moved to an inner-city neighborhood in Milwaukee, where her mother worked long hours as a maid. Around this time, Lee gave birth to Winfrey’s younger half-sister, Patricia, who died in 2003 from cocaine-related causes, and a third daughter also named Patricia, who was adopted to ease financial strain. Winfrey did not learn of her second half-sister until 2010. By 1962, Lee gave birth to Winfrey’s half-brother Jeffrey, who died of AIDS-related causes in 1989. At age eight, she was baptized in a Baptist church. Winfrey reported being molested by her cousin, uncle, and a family friend starting at age nine, which she first disclosed on a 1986 episode of her show. A biographer claimed that when she shared this with family at age 24, they refused to believe her. She once said she chose not to be a mother because she had not been mothered well. At age 13, after years of abuse, she ran away from home. At 14, she became pregnant, but her son was born prematurely and died shortly after. She later expressed betrayal over a family member who sold the story of her son to the National Enquirer in 1990. Winfrey attended Lincoln Middle and High School in Milwaukee, then transferred to Nicolet High School after early success in the Upward Bound program. She was reminded of her poverty on the bus, leading her to steal money from her mother to keep up with peers. Her mother sent her to live with Vernon in Nashville, where he was strict but encouraging and made education a priority. Winfrey became an honors student, was voted Most Popular Girl, and placed second nationally in dramatic interpretation. In 1986, she said, "When my father took me, it changed the course of my life. He saved me. He simply knew what he wanted and expected. He would take nothing less." Her first job was at a local grocery store. At 17, she won the Miss Black Tennessee pageant and gained attention from WVOL, a local black radio station, which hired her for part-time news work during high school and her first two years of college. She won an oratory contest, securing a full scholarship to Tennessee State University, a historically black institution, where she studied communication. She did not deliver her final paper until 1987, by which time she was a successful television personality, and only then earned her degree. Her grandmother once said that ever since Winfrey could talk, she was on stage, and she played games interviewing her corncob doll and crows. Winfrey acknowledged her grandmother’s influence, saying she encouraged her to speak in public and gave her a positive sense of self. Winfrey worked at WLAC-TV in Nashville as the youngest news anchor and the first black female news anchor, covering stories alongside John Tesh. In 1976, she moved to Baltimore’s WJZ-TV to co-anchor the six o’clock news, but was removed from that role and later joined Richard Sher as co-host of People Are Talking, which premiered on August 14, 1978. She also hosted Dialing for Dollars. In 1984, she moved to Chicago to host WLS-TV’s low-rated morning talk show, AM Chicago, which aired on January 2, 1984. Within months, the show rose from last place to overtaking Donahue as the highest-rated in Chicago. Roger Ebert persuaded her to sign a syndication deal with King World, predicting she would generate 40 times as much revenue as his show, At the Movies. The show was renamed The Oprah Winfrey Show and expanded to a full hour, with its first national broadcast on September 8, 1986. The syndicated show brought in double Donahue’s national audience, displacing him as the number-one daytime talk show in America. Time magazine noted that despite lacking journalistic toughness, Winfrey excelled in empathy, often making guests reveal personal stories they would not share with a national audience, likening the show to a group therapy session. Howard Rosenberg described her as "roundhouse, a full course meal, big, brassy, loud, aggressive, hyper, laughable, lovable, soulful, tender, low-down, earthy, and hungry," and said she may know Donahue’s jugular. Les Payne observed she was sharper, wittier, more genuine, and better attuned to her audience than Donahue, while Martha Bayles called her a relief for having cultural and religious roots. In the early years, the show was classified as a tabloid talk show. In the mid-1990s, Winfrey shifted focus to broader topics such as heart disease, geopolitics, spirituality, and meditation, interviewing celebrities on social issues like cancer, charity, and substance abuse, and hosting giveaways. Later, the show faced criticism for promoting junk science, particularly regarding guests like Jenny McCarthy’s unfounded claims about vaccines and Suzanne Somers’s promotion of bioidenticals. In addition to her talk show, Winfrey moderated three ABC Afterschool Specials from 1992 to 1994 and produced and co-starred in The Women of Brewster Place (1989) and its spin-off, Brewster Place. She co-founded Oxygen, the initial network for her Oprah After the Show program from 2002 to 2006, before moving to Oprah.com when she sold her stake. She is also president of Harpo Productions (Oprah spelled backwards), a production company behind The Oprah Winfrey Show, Dr. Phil, Rachael Ray, and The Dr. Oz Show. Dr. Phil has been criticized as simplistic or harmful, with the National Alliance on Mental Illness calling his conduct "unethical" and "incredibly irresponsible." Dr. Oz has been criticized by medical publications for spreading pseudoscience, including promoting "miracle pills" for weight loss. Science-Based Medicine stated no other TV show offers as much bad health advice as The Dr. Oz Show, all while appearing credible. Multiple publications have urged Winfrey to denounce medical statements made by former guests long after their shows ended, including calls to denounce Dr. Oz in 2020 over his coronavirus comments and promotion of a poorly vetted drug as a cure. On January 15, 2008, Winfrey and Discovery Communications announced plans to rebrand Discovery Health into the Oprah Winfrey Network (OWN), which was scheduled to launch in 2009 but delayed and officially launched on January 1, 2011. The final episode of The Oprah Winfrey Show aired on May 25, 2011. In January 2017, CBS announced Winfrey would join 60 Minutes as a special contributor starting in September 2017, and she left by the end of 2018. In June 2018, Apple announced a multi-year content partnership with Winfrey to create original programs for Apple TV+. The first show, Oprah's Book Club, premiered on November 1, 2019, based on a segment from her talk show. The second, Oprah Talks COVID-19, debuted on March 21, 2020, during the pandemic. A third show, The Oprah Conversation, premiered on July 30, 2020, to explore impactful topics with global thought leaders. In 1993, Winfrey hosted a prime-time interview with Michael Jackson titled Michael Jackson Talks ... to Oprah, which became the fourth most-watched event in American television history with 36.5 million viewers and the most-watched interview ever. On December 1, 2005, she appeared on The Late Show with David Letterman for the first time in 16 years to promote The Color Purple, which she produced. The episode was hailed as a "television event of the decade" and drew 13.45 million viewers, the largest audience in Letterman’s 11-year span. Although rumors of a feud were reported, both Winfrey and Letterman denied it, with Winfrey stating, "It's really over, whatever you thought was happening." On September 10, 2007, Letterman made his first appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show, as the season premiere was filmed in New York City. In 2006, rappers Ludacris, 50 Cent, and Ice Cube criticized Winfrey for what they saw as anti-hip hop bias. Ludacris said she gave him a hard time about his lyrics, edited comments during an appearance with the Crash cast, and did not initially invite him. Winfrey responded that she opposes rap lyrics that marginalize women but enjoys artists like Kanye West, and said she spoke with Ludacris backstage to explain her position, understanding his music was for entertainment but that some listeners might take it literally.

Both Winfrey and Letterman rejected discussions about a potential collaboration, with Winfrey stating, "I want you to know, it's really over, whatever you thought was happening." On September 10, 2007, Letterman made his first appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show, which was filmed in New York City. In 2006, rappers Ludacris, 50 Cent, and Ice Cube criticized Winfrey for what they saw as anti-hip hop bias; Ludacris claimed she gave him a hard time about his lyrics and edited comments he made during an appearance with the cast of Crash, and that he wasn't initially invited on the show. Winfrey responded by saying she opposes rap lyrics that "marginalize women" but enjoys artists like Kanye West, and that she spoke with Ludacris backstage to explain her position, acknowledging his music was for entertainment but noting some listeners might take it literally. In September 2008, Matt Drudge reported that Winfrey refused to have Sarah Palin on her show due to her support for Barack Obama; Winfrey denied the report, stating she had no discussion about Palin and that after publicly supporting Obama, she decided not to use her show as a platform for any candidates, though Obama appeared twice prior to his candidacy. She later said Palin would be a fantastic guest and did invite her on November 18, 2009. In 2009, Winfrey faced criticism for allowing actress Suzanne Somers to discuss hormone treatments not accepted by mainstream medicine, and critics suggested she is not tough enough when questioning guests she likes; Lisa de Moraes of The Washington Post noted that Oprah only asks follow-up questions of authors who have embarrassed her with fabricated memoirs, referencing James Frey's A Million Little Pieces. In 2021, Winfrey conducted a global interview with Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Prince Harry, which received international media attention. In 2024, ABC aired "AI and the Future of Us: An Oprah Winfrey Special," a one-hour show exploring artificial intelligence's impact on daily life, featuring interviews with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Bill Gates. Winfrey co-starred in Steven Spielberg's The Color Purple (1985) as Sofia, earning an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress; the Alice Walker novel later became a Broadway musical opening in late 2005 with Winfrey credited as a producer. In October 1998, Winfrey produced and starred in Beloved, based on Toni Morrison's Pulitzer Prize-winning novel; to prepare for her role as Sethe, she underwent a 24-hour simulation of slavery involving being tied up, blindfolded, and left alone in the woods. Despite major advertising and moderate to good reviews, the film opened to poor box-office results, losing approximately $30 million. Co-star Thandiwe Newton described Winfrey as "a very strong technical actress and it's because she's so smart. She's acute. She's got a mind like a razor blade." Harpo Films released a made-for-television film adaptation of Zora Neale Hurston's 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God in 2005, based on a teleplay by Suzan-Lori Parks and starring Halle Berry. In late 2008, Harpo Films signed an exclusive output pact with HBO to develop and produce scripted series, documentaries, and movies. In 2013, Winfrey starred in The Butler directed by Lee Daniels, which garnered significant Oscar buzz but did not result in a nomination. Winfrey voiced Gussie the goose in Charlotte's Web (2006) and Judge Bumbleton in Bee Movie (2007), co-starring Jerry Seinfeld and Renée Zellweger; in 2009, she voiced Eudora, the mother of Princess Tiana, in Disney's The Princess and the Frog, and in 2010 narrated the US version of the BBC nature program Life for Discovery. In 2018, she starred as Mrs. Which in the film adaptation of Madeleine L'Engle's A Wrinkle in Time and lent her voice to an animated virtual-reality short film written and directed by Eric Darnell, starring John Legend, titled Crow: The Legend, telling a Native American origin tale. Winfrey has co-authored five books; when her 2005 weight-loss book with Bob Greene was announced, it was reported that her undisclosed advance broke the world record for the highest book advance, previously held by Bill Clinton's autobiography. In 2015, her memoir The Life You Want was announced following a tour of the same name, scheduled for publication in 2017, but was "indefinitely postponed" in 2016. Winfrey publishes Oprah Daily and from 2004 to 2008 also published O At Home; in 2002, Fortune called O, the Oprah Magazine the most successful start-up in the industry; although circulation declined by over 10 percent to 2.4 million from 2005 to 2008, the January 2009 issue was the best-selling since 2006; the magazine's audience is more upscale than her TV show, with average readers earning above the U.S. median for women. In July 2020, it was announced that O Magazine would end regular print publications after the December 2020 issue; in that issue, Winfrey thanked readers and acknowledged it was the magazine's "final monthly print edition." Winfrey's company created Oprah.com, which averages over 70 million page views and more than six million users per month, receiving about 20,000 emails weekly; she initiated "Oprah's Child Predator Watch List" through her show and website, leading to the capture of two men within 48 hours. On February 9, 2006, Winfrey signed a three-year, $55-million contract with XM Satellite Radio to launch Oprah Radio, featuring contributors like Nate Berkus, Dr. Mehmet Oz, Bob Greene, Dr. Robin Smith, and Marianne Williamson; Oprah & Friends began broadcasting at 11:00 a.m. ET on September 25, 2006, from a new studio in Chicago, airing 24 hours a day, seven days a week on XM Channel 156; the contract requires her to be on air 30 minutes a week, 39 weeks a year. Winfrey's extensive real-estate portfolio has drawn attention, with industry outlets calling her a "tycoon," and her investments estimated at approximately $127 million as of 2022. She first purchased a condominium in Chicago's Water Tower Place in 1985, then bought adjoining units in 1992, 1993, and 1994. In 1988, she bought a 164-acre property in Rolling Prairie, Indiana, including main and guest residences, orchard, and stables. In 1992, she purchased an 80-acre compound in Telluride, Colorado, which she sold around late 2000. In 1994, she bought an apartment at the Four Seasons Hotel Chicago. Between 1996 and 2000, she purchased five condos in Fisher Island, Florida. In 2000, through her Chicago-based LLC Overground Railroad, she purchased an estate in Greenwich, Connecticut for her friend Gayle King. In 2001, she sold all five Fisher Island condos and bought what became her "main home base," called "The Promised Land," a 42-acre estate with ocean and mountain views in Montecito, California, as of 2022. That year, she also purchased homes in Elmwood Park, Illinois, and Merrillville, Indiana for family and friends. In 2002, she bought her father's home in Franklin, Tennessee and a lakefront condo in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. In 2003, she listed her Rolling Prairie property and sold it in 2004. From 2003 to 2005, she acquired several properties totaling 163 acres in Kula and Hana, Hawaii, and a penthouse in Atlanta, Georgia. In 2005, she purchased a home in Douglasville, Georgia, which was gifted in 2011 to a family member. In 2006, she bought a co-op apartment along Lake Shore Drive in downtown Chicago, reportedly with plans to move permanently from her Water Tower Place unit; for unknown reasons, it remained unused until sold in 2012. In 2008, she sold her Atlanta penthouse and listed Gayle King's estate, then purchased a penthouse in midtown Manhattan through her second LLC, Sophie's Penthouse, which was later sold in 2012. In early 2014, she listed her Chicago duplex; later that year, she returned to Telluride to buy a 60-acre lot with plans to build, and a lawsuit by a retired nuclear physicist over trail access rights was dismissed due to lack of case law and other issues; the extent of the agreement remains undisclosed. In 2015, she purchased another property in Telluride, expanded her Montecito compound by 23 acres, and acquired another 44-acre dedicated crop and equestrian preserve; she also sold both of her downtown Chicago homes. In 2018, she obtained two adjoining parcels totaling 23 acres including the Madroneagle compound on Orcas Island, Washington, and sold her last Chicago-area home in Elmwood Park. In late 2019, she expanded her Montecito home-base to 70 contiguous acres by purchasing a four-acre complex from actor Jeff Bridges. In 2021, she sold her Orcas Island compound as she said she was too busy to use it and purchased another compound in Montecito further from her main base, flipping the latter in 2022 with split properties—one sold to her property manager and longtime personal trainer Bob Greene, the other to actress Jennifer Aniston. In 2023, Winfrey purchased 870 acres of land in Maui for $6.6 million. Winfrey's high school sweetheart Anthony Otey recalled an innocent courtship beginning in her senior year, during which he saved hundreds of love notes; she conducted herself with dignity and was a model student. The two spoke of marriage, but Otey claimed he always knew she was destined for a greater life than he could provide; she broke up with him on Valentine's Day of her senior year. In 1971, months after ending her relationship with Otey, Winfrey met William "Bubba" Taylor at Tennessee State University, whom CBS journalist George Mair described as her "first intense, to-die-for love affair"; Winfrey helped get Taylor a job at WVOL and "did everything to keep him, including literally begging him on her knees to stay with her." Taylor refused to leave Nashville when she moved to Baltimore to work at WJZ-TV in June 1976; Winfrey later recalled they shared a deep love and that she would never forget it. In the 1970s, Winfrey had a romantic relationship with John Tesh; biographer Kitty Kelley claims Tesh ended the relationship due to pressures of an interracial relationship. When WJZ-TV management criticized Winfrey for crying on air during tragedies and her hair falling out from a bad perm, she turned to reporter Lloyd Kramer for comfort; she later recalled Kramer was "the best," loved her even when bald, and was the most fun romance she ever had. According to Mair, when Kramer moved to NBC in New York, Winfrey had a love affair with a married man who had no intention of leaving his wife; she recalled being with him for four years, never living with him, and feeling powerless and depleted, eventually pleading on her knees; on September 8, 1981, she wrote a suicide note to best friend Gayle King instructing her to water her plants. Winfrey later said the suicide note was "much overplayed" and that she couldn't kill herself because she feared missing something good. She attributed her weight gain and history of abusive relationships to a deep need for approval and self-worth, saying she would accept cruel self-absorbed men's criticism because she didn't believe she deserved anything else, and that this was also how she cushioned against disapproval. Winfrey later confessed to smoking crack cocaine with a man she was romantically involved with during that era, explaining that she was addicted to the man, not the drug, and that she would have done anything for him. She was allegedly involved in a second drug-related relationship with Randolph Cook, who claimed they lived together for several months in 1985 and used drugs; in 1997, Cook sued Winfrey for $20 million over an alleged tell-all book about their relationship. In the mid-1980s, Winfrey briefly dated movie critic Roger Ebert, whom she credits with advising her to take her show into syndication. In 1985, before her Chicago talk show went national, Haitian filmmaker Reginald Chevalier claims he appeared in a look-alike segment and began a relationship with Winfrey involving romantic evenings, candlelit baths, and dinners with Michael Jordan and Danny Glover; Chevalier says Winfrey ended the relationship when she met Stedman Graham. Winfrey and her partner Stedman Graham have been together since 1986; they were engaged in November 1992, but the ceremony never took place. Winfrey's best friend since their early twenties is Gayle King, who was formerly the host of The Gayle King Show and is currently an editor of O, the Oprah Magazine; since 1997, when Winfrey played the therapist on an episode of the sitcom Ellen.

Oprah Winfrey has faced legal threats, with one individual suing her for $20 million, alleging she blocked the publication of a tell-all book about their alleged relationship. In the mid-1980s, Winfrey briefly dated movie critic Roger Ebert, whom she credits with advising her to take her talk show into syndication. In 1985, before her show went national, Haitian filmmaker Reginald Chevalier claims he appeared in a look-alike segment and began a romantic relationship with Winfrey, which included evenings at home, candlelit baths, and dinners with Michael Jordan and Danny Glover; he says Winfrey ended the relationship when she met Stedman Graham. Winfrey and Stedman Graham have been together since 1986 and were engaged in November 1992, though the ceremony never occurred. Winfrey's best friend since their early twenties is Gayle King, who previously hosted The Gayle King Show and is now an editor of O, the Oprah Magazine. Since 1997, when Winfrey played therapist in an episode of Ellen in which Ellen DeGeneres came out, the two have been the subject of persistent rumors they are gay; Winfrey acknowledges the cultural lack of definition for such a close female bond and states she is not ashamed of being gay. Winfrey has also maintained a long friendship with Maria Shriver, whom she met in Baltimore, and considers Maya Angelou, author of I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, her mentor and close friend, calling her "mother-sister-friend." In 1998, Winfrey hosted a week-long Caribbean cruise for Angelou and 150 guests to celebrate her 70th birthday and in 2008, threw her an extravagant 80th birthday celebration at Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. Raised in rural poverty by a mother dependent on government welfare in a poor urban neighborhood, Winfrey became a millionaire at age 32 when her show received national syndication. She negotiated ownership rights and founded her own production company. At age 41, her net worth was $340 million, making her the only African American on the Forbes 400; by 2000, her net worth reached $800 million, and she is believed to have been the richest African American of the 20th century. A course on her business acumen, "History 298: Oprah Winfrey, the Tycoon," is taught at the University of Illinois. In 2006, Winfrey was the highest-paid television entertainer in the U.S., earning an estimated $260 million—five times more than second-place music executive Simon Cowell—and by 2008, her yearly income had increased to $275 million. Forbes listed her as the world's only black billionaire from 2004 to 2006 and recognized her as the first black woman billionaire in 2003. As of 2014, her net worth exceeded $2.9 billion, and she overtook former eBay CEO Meg Whitman as the richest self-made woman in America. Winfrey was raised a Baptist and has spoken about her faith, stating she believes in a "God force" that lives within all people and that doubt is a signal to pause and reflect. She cites Acts 17:28 as her favorite Bible verse and attends The Potter's House, an Evangelical church in Dallas. After losing her infant child at age 14, Winfrey did not want more children, explaining in a 2017 Vanity Fair interview that she lacks the patience for babies, though she has patience for puppies. Winfrey has been called "arguably the world's most powerful woman" by CNN and TIME, "arguably the most influential woman in the world" by The American Spectator, and "one of the 100 people who most influenced the 20th Century" and "one of the most influential people" from 2004 to 2011 by TIME—being the only person to appear on the latter list ten times. At the end of the 20th century, Life named her the most influential woman and most influential black person of her generation, calling her "America's most powerful woman"; in 2007, USA Today ranked her the most influential woman and most influential black person of the previous quarter-century. Ladies' Home Journal ranked her number one among the most powerful women in America, and Senator Barack Obama said in 2007 she "may be the most influential woman in the country." In 1998, Winfrey became the first woman and first African American to top Entertainment Weekly's list of the 101 most powerful people in entertainment. Forbes named her the world's most powerful celebrity in 2005, 2007, 2008, 2010, and 2013. As chairman of Harpo Inc., she was named the most powerful woman in entertainment by The Hollywood Reporter in 2008. She has been listed as one of the world's 100 most powerful women by Forbes, ranking 14th in 2014 and 31st in 2023. In 2010, Life named her one of the 100 people who changed the world, alongside Jesus Christ, Elvis Presley, and Lady Mary Wortley Montagu—she was the only living woman on the list. Columnist Maureen Dowd called her the "top alpha female" in the country, stating she has more credibility than the president and that no other successful woman had to be publicly criticized to advance. Vanity Fair claimed Oprah has more cultural influence than any university president, politician, or religious leader except perhaps the Pope. Bill O'Reilly described her as a woman who rose from nothing to become the most powerful woman in the world, noting her loyal following, credibility, talent, and self-made success. In 2005, Winfrey was named the greatest woman in American history in a public poll as part of The Greatest American, ranking No. 9 overall. Polls on her popularity have been inconsistent: a November 2003 Gallup poll found 73% of Americans had a favorable view of her, which rose to 74% in January 2007 but dropped to 66% in October 2007 and to 55% in a December 2007 Fox News poll. Gallup consistently ranks her among the most admired women in the world, with her highest rating in 2007 when she was tied with Hillary Clinton for first place. In a 2010 New Statesman list, she was ranked 38th in "The World's 50 Most Influential Figures 2010." In 1989, she was inducted into the NAACP Image Award Hall of Fame. The Wall Street Journal coined the term "Oprahfication," referring to public confession as therapy. By sharing intimate details about her weight, love life, and sexual abuse and crying with guests, Winfrey is credited by Time with creating "rapport talk," distinct from Phil Donahue's "report talk," emphasizing the emotional connection between viewer and host. Observers have noted the "Oprahfication" of politics, including "Oprah-style debates," and Bill Clinton being described as "the man who brought Oprah-style psychobabble and misty confessions to politics." Newsweek stated that every time a politician shows emotion or a cable anchor "emotes," they are nodding to the cult of confession Oprah helped create. The November 1988 Ms. magazine noted that in a society where fat is taboo, Winfrey made it sexy, elegant, and nearly gorgeous through her wardrobe and sensuality. While Phil Donahue pioneered the tabloid talk show genre, Winfrey's warmth, intimacy, and personal confession popularized and transformed it. In the book Freaks Talk Back, Yale professor Joshua Gamson credits the genre with providing high-impact media visibility for LGBT people and making them more socially acceptable than any other 20th-century development. Michael Bronski wrote that before tabloid talk shows, LGBT people had almost no presence on television, and shows like Jerry Springer, Jenny Jones, Oprah, and Geraldo brought them into living rooms daily. Gamson believes these shows helped make alternative sexual identities more acceptable in mainstream society, contributing to increased gay visibility and declining suicide rates. In April 1997, Winfrey played therapist in "The Puppy Episode" on Ellen, where the character and real-life Ellen DeGeneres came out as a lesbian. The power of Winfrey's opinions and endorsements to influence public opinion—especially consumer behavior—has been dubbed "the Oprah Effect." This influence has been documented in book sales, beef markets, and election voting. In late 1996, Winfrey launched the Oprah's Book Club segment, which focused on new and classic books and brought obscure novels to prominence; when she selected East of Eden, it soared to the top of the charts. Being recognized by her often leads to a million additional book sales. In Reading with Oprah: The Book Club that Changed America (2005), Kathleen Rooney describes her as a serious American intellectual who used electronic media to promote reading and motivate millions of non-readers. When Jonathan Franzen's book was selected, he reportedly "cringed" and said such selections tend to be "schmaltzy." After James Frey's A Million Little Pieces was found to contain fabrications in 2006, Winfrey confronted him on her show over the breach of trust, and in 2009 apologized to Frey. During a 1996 show on mad cow disease with Howard Lyman, Winfrey said she was stopped from eating another burger; Texas cattlemen sued her and Lyman in early 1998 for "false defamation of perishable food" and "business disparagement," claiming their remarks caused cattle prices to fall and cost producers $11 million. Winfrey was represented by attorney Chip Babcock, and after a two-month trial in Amarillo, Texas, a jury found her and Lyman not liable. Her success in launching other talk shows such as Dr. Phil, The Dr. Oz Show, and Rachael Ray has also been cited as evidence of "The Oprah Effect." Matthew Baum and Angela Jamison conducted a study showing that politically unaware individuals who watch soft news shows like The Oprah Winfrey Show are 14% more likely to vote consistently than those who only watch hard news. Winfrey identifies as a political independent who says she "earned the right to think for myself and to vote for myself." She endorsed Barack Obama in the 2008 presidential election, making her first public endorsement on Larry King Live in September 2006. Two economists estimate her endorsement was worth over a million votes in the Democratic primary and that without it, Obama would have lost the nomination. She held a fundraiser for Obama at her Santa Barbara estate in September 2007 and joined him in rallies in Iowa, New Hampshire, and South Carolina in December 2007, with the Columbia event drawing nearly 30,000 attendees—the largest political event of 2007. An analysis by economists at the University of Maryland estimated her endorsement caused between 420,000 and 1.6 million votes for Obama in the Democratic primary, based on states excluding Texas, Michigan, North Dakota, Kansas, and Alaska, and that it contributed to the popular vote difference between Obama and Hillary Clinton. Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich said Winfrey's endorsement was so impactful he considered offering her his vacant Senate seat, calling her "the most instrumental person in electing Barack Obama president" with a voice "larger than all 100 senators combined." Winfrey responded by stating she was not interested in being a senator but did feel she could be one. The Topps trading card company honored her involvement in the campaign by featuring her on a card in a set commemorating Obama.

Oprah Winfrey drew a crowd of nearly 30,000 at a political event in 2007, the largest for any political event that year. An analysis by two economists at the University of Maryland, College Park estimated that Winfrey's endorsement was responsible for between 420,000 and 1,600,000 votes for Barack Obama in the Democratic primary, based on a sample of states excluding Texas, Michigan, North Dakota, Kansas, and Alaska. The results indicate that Winfrey's endorsement accounted for the difference in the popular vote between Obama and Hillary Clinton. Illinois Governor Rod Blagojevich stated he considered offering Winfrey Obama's vacant Senate seat, calling her "the most instrumental person in electing Barack Obama president" and saying she had "a voice larger than all 100 senators combined." Winfrey responded that while she was not interested in running for Senate, she did feel she could be a senator. Topps trading card company featured Winfrey on a card in a set commemorating Obama's road to the White House. In April 2014, Winfrey spoke for over 20 minutes at a fundraiser in Arlington, Virginia, for Lavern Chatman, a Democratic primary candidate, despite reports that Chatman had been found liable in 2001 for defrauding hundreds of District of Columbia nursing-home employees of at least $1.4 million in owed wages. Winfrey endorsed Hillary Clinton in the 2016 election and referred to Donald Trump as a "demagogue." In 2018, she canvassed door-to-door for Georgia gubernatorial Democratic nominee Stacey Abrams and donated $500,000 to the March for Our Lives student demonstration advocating for gun control. Media speculation about Winfrey running for president, especially in the lead-up to the 2020 election, was noted, but she denied any plans, stating in 2018 that while it was "a humbling thing to have people think you can run the country," she "would not be able to do it. It's not a clean business. It would kill me." She suggested she would publicly endorse a candidate in the 2020 Democratic primaries but ultimately did not. She later campaigned for Joe Biden during the general election. In early 2018, Winfrey met with Mohammad bin Salman, the crown prince and de facto ruler of Saudi Arabia, during his visit to the United States. In the 2022 Pennsylvania Senate election, she endorsed Democrat John Fetterman over Republican Mehmet Oz, whose show she promoted. In the 2022 Maryland gubernatorial election, she endorsed Baltimore author Wes Moore in the Democratic primary and co-hosted a virtual fundraiser for him in June. She attended and spoke at Moore's gubernatorial inauguration on January 18, 2023. In 2022, Winfrey established OWN Your Vote, a nonpartisan group focused on voter registration and a get-out-the-vote campaign aimed at providing Black women with tools and resources to vote in the November election. The group's partners include Advancement Project, African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME), Color Of Change, Delta Sigma Theta sorority, The King Center, The Lawyers' Committee, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, National Action Network, National Bar Association, National Council of Negro Women, Sigma Gamma Rho, Southern Poverty Law Center, VoteRunLead, and Vote.org. On August 21, 2024, Winfrey endorsed Kamala Harris at the 2024 Democratic National Convention. In 2000, she received the Spingarn Medal from the NAACP. In 2002, Christianity Today published an article titled "The Church of O," concluding that Winfrey had become an influential spiritual leader, noting that since 1994, when she shifted to more edifying content, and 1998, when she launched "Change Your Life TV," her most significant role became that of a spiritual leader. The article described her as a "postmodern priestess—an icon of church-free spirituality" to her audience of over 22 million mostly female viewers. This sentiment was echoed by Marcia Z. Nelson in her book The Gospel According to Oprah. Since the mid-1990s, Winfrey's show has emphasized uplifting and inspirational topics, and some viewers say it has motivated them to perform acts of altruism, such as helping Congolese women and building an orphanage. A scientific study by psychological scientists at the University of Cambridge, University of Plymouth, and University of California found that watching an uplifting clip from The Oprah Winfrey Show caused subjects to become twice as helpful as those who watched a British comedy or nature documentary. In 1998, Winfrey began an ongoing conversation with Gary Zukav, a spiritual teacher, who appeared on her show 35 times. Winfrey keeps a copy of Zukav's The Seat of the Soul at her bedside, calling it one of her all-time favorites. On the premiere of her 13th season, Roseanne Barr told Winfrey "you're the African Mother Goddess of us all," which inspired enthusiasm from the studio audience. The animated series Futurama referenced her spiritual influence by suggesting "Oprahism" is a mainstream religion in 3000 AD. Twelve days after the September 11 attacks, New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani asked Winfrey to host a Prayer for America service at Yankee Stadium, attended by former President Bill Clinton and Senator Hillary Clinton. Leading up to the U.S.-led 2001 invasion of Afghanistan, less than a month after September 11, Winfrey aired a controversial show called "Islam 101," portraying Islam as a religion of peace and calling it "the most misunderstood of the three major religions." In 2002, George W. Bush invited Winfrey to join a U.S. delegation including adviser Karen Hughes and Condoleezza Rice to go to Afghanistan to celebrate the return of Afghan girls to school; the "Oprah strategy" aimed to portray the war on terror positively, but when Winfrey refused to participate, the trip was postponed. Leading up to the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, Winfrey's show faced criticism for allegedly having an anti-war bias. Ben Shapiro of Townhall.com wrote that Winfrey was a "dangerous political force" with "unpredictable and mercurial attitudes." In 2006, Winfrey recalled receiving intense hate mail, including "Go back to Africa" messages, after a show titled "Is War the Only Answer?" which she said led to accusations of being un-American. Filmmaker Michael Moore defended Winfrey for showing antiwar footage that other media avoided and begged her to run for president. A February 2003 series, in which Winfrey showed clips from people worldwide urging America not to go to war, was interrupted in several East Coast markets by network broadcasts of a press conference by President George W. Bush and Colin Powell summarizing the case for war. In 2007, Winfrey began endorsing the self-help program The Secret, which claims people can change their lives through positive thoughts or 'vibrations' that attract more positive outcomes. Peter Birkenhead of Salon argued this idea is pseudoscience and psychologically damaging, promoting a quick-fix material culture, and criticized Winfrey's promotion as irresponsible. In 2007, skeptic and magician James Randi accused Winfrey of being deliberately deceptive and uncritical in handling paranormal claims on her show. In 2008, Winfrey endorsed author and spiritual teacher Eckhart Tolle and his book A New Earth: Awakening to Your Life's Purpose, which sold several million extra copies after being selected for her book club. During a webinar promoting the book, Winfrey stated "God is a feeling experience and not a believing experience. If your religion is a believing experience [...] then that's not truly God." Christian radio host Frank Pastore criticized Winfrey's views, saying if she is a Christian, she is "an ignorant one because Christianity is incompatible with New Age thought." In 2008, Winfrey was named Person of the Year by PETA for using her fame to help the less fortunate, including animals, and for exposing cruelty in puppy mills and factory farms, and for promoting a cruelty-free vegan diet. In 2009, Winfrey filmed interviews in Denmark highlighting its citizens as the happiest people in the world. In 2010, Bill O'Reilly of Fox News criticized these shows for promoting a left-wing society. Following the launch of Super Soul Sunday and SuperSoul Sessions on Harpo Productions' SuperSoul TV in 2016, Winfrey selected 100 people for the SuperSoul 100 list of innovators and visionaries aligned on a mission to move humanity forward. On the use of the N-word, Winfrey said, "You cannot be my friend and use that word around me. ... I always think of the people who heard that as their last word as they were hanging from a tree." The viewership for The Oprah Winfrey Show peaked during the 1991–92 season at about 13.1 million daily viewers. By 2003, ratings declined to 7.4 million daily viewers. Ratings briefly rose to about 9 million in 2005 and then declined to around 7.3 million in 2008, though the show remained the highest-rated talk show. In 2008, the show was airing in 140 countries and reached an estimated 46 million people weekly in the U.S. According to Harris poll data, Winfrey was America's favorite television personality in 1998, 2000, 2002–06, and 2009, especially among women, Democrats, political moderates, Baby Boomers, Generation X, Southern Americans, and East Coast Americans. Outside the U.S., Winfrey became increasingly popular in the Arab world; in 2007, MBC 4, an Arab satellite channel, centered its programming around reruns of her show due to record female viewership in Saudi Arabia. In 2008, The New York Times reported that The Oprah Winfrey Show with Arabic subtitles aired twice each weekday on MBC 4. Winfrey's modest dress and attitude of triumph over adversity and abuse have caused some women in Saudi Arabia to idealize her. In 2004, Winfrey became the first Black person to rank among the 50 most generous Americans and remained in the top 50 until 2010. By 2012, she had given away about $400 million to educational causes. As of 2012, she had also given over 400 scholarships to Morehouse College in Atlanta, Georgia. Winfrey received the first Bob Hope Humanitarian Award at the 2002 Emmy Awards for services to television and film. To celebrate two decades on national TV and thank her employees, Winfrey took her staff and their families (1,065 people total) on vacation to Hawaii in summer 2006. In 2013, Winfrey donated $12 million to the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom that same year. Winfrey purchased 2,130 acres of land in Maui and established a bed and breakfast for entertaining friends and a (unprofitable) organic farm dedicated to keeping the area unoccupied and growing native species to restore damaged watersheds. She distributed pillows, diapers, and other supplies to survivors of a devastating fire and, with Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson, set up the People’s Fund of Maui, personally donating $25 million. In 1998, Winfrey created Oprah's Angel Network, a charity that supported charitable projects and provided grants to nonprofit organizations worldwide. The network raised over $80 million ($1 million from Jon Bon Jovi), with Winfrey covering all administrative costs so 100% of funds went to charity programs. In May 2010, with the end of her show, the charity stopped accepting donations and was shut down. In 2004, Winfrey and her team filmed an episode titled "Oprah's Christmas Kindness" in South Africa, traveling to bring attention to children affected by poverty and AIDS. During a 21-day trip, Winfrey and her crew visited schools and orphanages, distributing Christmas presents to 50,000 children—dolls for girls and soccer balls for boys, along with school supplies. Throughout the show, Winfrey appealed to viewers to donate to Oprah's Angel Network for poor and AIDS-affected children in Africa. From that show alone, viewers donated over $7 million. Winfrey invested $40 million and some of her time to establish the Oprah Winfrey Leadership Academy for Girls in Henley on Klip, south of Johannesburg, South Africa. The school, spanning 22 acres, opened in January 2007 with 150 pupils (increasing to 450) and includes state-of-the-art classrooms, computer and science labs, a library, a theater, and a beauty salon. Nelson Mandela praised Winfrey for overcoming her own disadvantaged youth to become a benefactor. Critics viewed the school as elitist and unnecessarily luxurious. Winfrey rejected these claims, saying, "If you are surrounded by beautiful things and wonderful teachers who inspire you, that beauty brings out the beauty in you." Winfrey, who has no surviving biological children, described maternal feelings toward the girls at the academy. She teaches a class at the school via satellite.
